latest_nl_proof:
Using the standard definition, a numerical semigroup is a cofinite additive submonoid of N0; m(S) is its least positive element, and g(S) is the number of gaps, i.e. the size of N0 minus S.

Define φ : A_{m,g} → K_{m,g} as follows. Let S ∈ A_{m,g}. For each i ∈ {1,...,m-1}, because S is cofinite, the set T_i = { s ∈ S : s is congruent to i modulo m } is nonempty; being a nonempty subset of N0, it has a least element. Call that least element w_i. Since w_i is congruent to i modulo m, there is an integer k_i ≥ 0 with w_i = k_i m + i. In fact k_i ≥ 1: if k_i = 0 then w_i = i, so i ∈ S with 0 < i < m, contradicting m(S)=m. Set φ(S) = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}).

We show φ(S) ∈ K_{m,g}. First, the Kunz inequalities. Fix integers i,j with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1.
If i+j < m, then w_i + w_j ∈ S and is congruent to i+j modulo m. Since w_{i+j} is the least element of S in that residue class, w_i + w_j ≥ w_{i+j}. Substituting w_r = k_r m + r gives
(k_i + k_j)m + (i+j) ≥ k_{i+j}m + (i+j),
so k_i + k_j ≥ k_{i+j}.
If i+j > m, then w_i + w_j ∈ S and is congruent to i+j-m modulo m, so w_i + w_j ≥ w_{i+j-m}. Now
w_i + w_j = (k_i + k_j)m + (i+j) = (k_i + k_j + 1)m + (i+j-m),
whence
(k_i + k_j + 1)m + (i+j-m) ≥ k_{i+j-m}m + (i+j-m),
so k_i + k_j + 1 ≥ k_{i+j-m}.
Thus all defining inequalities of K_{m,g} hold.

Next, the sum condition. For each i ∈ {1,...,m-1}, the nonnegative integers congruent to i modulo m that are not in S are exactly
i, m+i, 2m+i, ..., (k_i-1)m+i.
Indeed, if 0 ≤ q < k_i, then qm+i < w_i and has the same residue class as w_i, so qm+i is not in S. Conversely, if q ≥ k_i, then
qm+i = w_i + (q-k_i)m,
and both w_i and m lie in S, so qm+i ∈ S. Also every multiple of m lies in S, because 0,m ∈ S and S is closed under addition. Therefore the gaps of S are partitioned by the residue classes 1,...,m-1, with exactly k_i gaps in residue class i. Hence
g(S) = k_1 + ... + k_{m-1}.
Since S ∈ A_{m,g}, we have g(S)=g, so k_1 + ... + k_{m-1} = g. Therefore φ(S) ∈ K_{m,g}.

Now define ψ : K_{m,g} → A_{m,g}. For k = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) ∈ K_{m,g}, let
S_k = {0} ∪ { qm : q is a nonnegative integer and q ≥ 1 } ∪ { qm+i : 1 ≤ i ≤ m-1, q is a nonnegative integer, and q ≥ k_i }.
We prove that S_k is a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m and genus g.

First, S_k is cofinite, because its complement in N0 consists exactly of the numbers qm+i with 1 ≤ i ≤ m-1 and 0 ≤ q < k_i, which form a finite set. So it remains to prove closure under addition. Let x,y ∈ S_k.
If one of x,y is a multiple of m, say x = ℓm with ℓ a nonnegative integer, then x+y is still in S_k: if y is also a multiple of m this is obvious, and if y = bm+j with 1 ≤ j ≤ m-1 and b ≥ k_j, then x+y = (ℓ+b)m + j, and ℓ+b ≥ b ≥ k_j.
Now assume neither x nor y is a multiple of m. Write
x = am+i,  y = bm+j,
with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ m-1, a ≥ k_i, and b ≥ k_j. By commutativity we may assume i ≤ j. There are three cases.
If i+j < m, then a+b ≥ k_i + k_j ≥ k_{i+j}, so
x+y = (a+b)m + (i+j) ∈ S_k.
If i+j = m, then x+y = (a+b+1)m ∈ S_k.
If i+j > m, then a+b+1 ≥ k_i + k_j + 1 ≥ k_{i+j-m}, so
x+y = (a+b+1)m + (i+j-m) ∈ S_k.
Thus S_k is closed under addition. Since it is an additive submonoid of N0 with finite complement, it is a numerical semigroup.

Its multiplicity is m. Indeed, m ∈ S_k, while for each i with 1 ≤ i ≤ m-1, the number i is not in S_k because k_i is positive. Hence no positive integer less than m belongs to S_k, so the least positive element of S_k is exactly m.

Its genus is g. The complement of S_k in N0 consists exactly of the numbers qm+i with 1 ≤ i ≤ m-1 and 0 ≤ q < k_i, so
g(S_k) = k_1 + ... + k_{m-1} = g.
Therefore S_k ∈ A_{m,g}, so ψ is well-defined.

Finally, φ and ψ are inverse maps.
Take S ∈ A_{m,g}, and let φ(S) = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}). From the description above, for each i ∈ {1,...,m-1}, the elements of S congruent to i modulo m are exactly the numbers qm+i with q ≥ k_i; and every multiple of m is in S. Hence S is exactly the set S_{(k_1,...,k_{m-1})} = ψ(φ(S)). So ψ∘φ is the identity on A_{m,g}.
Conversely, take k ∈ K_{m,g}. In S_k, the least element congruent to i modulo m is exactly k_i m + i, because qm+i is excluded for q < k_i and included for q = k_i. Therefore φ(S_k) = k. So φ∘ψ is the identity on K_{m,g}.

Hence φ is a bijection between A_{m,g} and K_{m,g}. Since N(m,g) = |A_{m,g}| by definition, it follows that N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.
role_in_parent: Transfers the counting problem from numerical semigroups to Kunz-coordinate tuples.
statement_nl: Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples k = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) of positive integers such that: (i) for all integers i,j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, if i + j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}; and (ii) k_1 + ... + k_{m-1} = g. Also define A_{m,g} to be the set of all numerical semigroups S with multiplicity m(S)=m and genus g(S)=g, and define N(m,g)=|A_{m,g}|. Then there exists a bijection between A_{m,g} and K_{m,g}. Consequently N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m ≥ 2
g is an integer with g ≥ 0
For K_{m,g}: each coordinate k_t is a positive integer for t ∈ {1,...,m-1}
For K_{m,g}: indices i,j satisfy 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1
For K_{m,g}: inequalities are applied only in the stated cases i+j < m and i+j > m
For A_{m,g}: S ranges over numerical semigroups (implicit: standard definition)
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers m,g with m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0, define K_{m,g} as the set of (m−1)-tuples k=(k_1,...,k_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying: (∀ i,j with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m−1) if i+j<m then k_i+k_j ≥ k_{i+j}, and if i+j>m then k_i+k_j+1 ≥ k_{i+j-m}; and additionally k_1+...+k_{m-1}=g. Define A_{m,g} as the set of numerical semigroups S with multiplicity m(S)=m and genus g(S)=g, and N(m,g)=|A_{m,g}|. Then there exists a bijection φ: A_{m,g} → K_{m,g}, hence N(m,g)=|K_{m,g}|.
quantifier_order: Fix m ∈ Z with m ≥ 2 and g ∈ Z with g ≥ 0
Define K_{m,g} = { k ∈ (Z_{>0})^{m-1} : (∀ i,j ∈ Z with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1, casewise inequalities hold) ∧ (k_1+...+k_{m-1}=g) }
Define A_{m,g} = { S : S is a numerical semigroup, m(S)=m, g(S)=g }
∃ a bijection φ such that φ: A_{m,g} → K_{m,g} is bijective
